name: MCL — superficial
description: Layer 2 of the medial knee: a flat band about 9.5 cm long from the medial epicondyle to the proximal tibia, deep to the pes anserinus. Thin, uniformly low signal and best seen on coronal images.

normal_values.femoral_attachment_center: about 3 mm proximal and 5 mm posterior to the medial epicondyle, or centered on it, in cadaver series

variants_pitfalls: On fat-sat images only a thin, sharp fluid line between the superficial and deep layers is normal; ill-defined fluid-bright signal around the sMCL is edema. Grade 1: edema around a normal ligament; grade 2: intrasubstance signal or partial disruption; grade 3: complete discontinuity.
Edema around the MCL without trauma is common in medial osteoarthritis (27 of 30 knees in one series): not a sprain without a valgus injury.
Distal tears hide: a wavy sMCL suggests a tibial-side tear, and a stump flipped superficial to the pes tendons (Stener-like lesion) blocks healing.
Pellegrini–Stieda ossification near the medial epicondyle marks an old proximal MCL injury; it can lie in the adductor magnus tendon instead.
The sMCL was injured in 62% of clinically isolated ACL ruptures in one series; check it on every ACL tear.
